questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes over-provisioning from under-provisioning when sizing compute for a new deployment, per Lesson 3?
options: Over-provisioning quietly wastes budget every month since the extra capacity sits unused; under-provisioning risks a real outage once real load exceeds what the infrastructure can handle
Under-provisioning quietly wastes budget every month, while over-provisioning risks a real outage
Both mistakes only ever show up as a wasted line item on a monthly bill, never as an outage
Over-provisioning is the correct default for any workload whose real load hasn't been measured yet
Under-provisioning only matters for workloads that have a compliance requirement
questions.explain: Lesson 3 is explicit that these are two different kinds of damage, not interchangeable labels: over-provisioning is a cost with no corresponding benefit, showing up as a wasted line item every month, while under-provisioning is a failure mode, showing up as a real outage the moment traffic exceeds capacity, often at the worst possible time.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B reverses which mistake causes which kind of damage — it's under-provisioning that risks a real outage when load exceeds capacity, while over-provisioning is the one that quietly wastes budget every month with no corresponding benefit. Swapping which direction causes an outage versus which direction wastes money is exactly the mix-up Lesson 3 warns against.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly defines a requirements brief, as covered in Lesson 1?
options: A short written record of a workload's expected load, compliance needs, budget, availability target, and user base, gathered before any infrastructure is chosen
A formal contract signed with the cloud provider guaranteeing a specific uptime percentage
The architecture diagram drawn after compute and storage have already been deployed
A list of the specific VM sizes and storage tiers a team plans to provision
A retrospective document written after an outage, explaining what should have been asked beforehand
questions.explain: Lesson 1's five questions — expected load, compliance requirements, budget, availability needs, and who the users are — are exactly what a requirements brief answers, in writing, before a single resource is provisioned. Every later decision in the chapter (provider, sizing, architecture) uses that brief as its input.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D describes a sizing decision, which is Lesson 3's job and comes after the requirements brief exists — the brief itself is about business constraints like load, compliance, budget, and availability, not a list of VM sizes or storage tiers someone has already chosen.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about choosing Azure, AWS, or both for a given workload, per Lesson 2.
options: Existing team expertise is a real cost factor — ramp-up time and slower incident response on an unfamiliar platform both have a dollar value
The provider that's cheaper in general is always the right choice for every workload, regardless of that workload's specific usage pattern
A genuine multi-cloud setup often traces back to inherited infrastructure from a merger or acquisition nobody has had the time to consolidate
Vendor lock-in is never a legitimate reason to choose a provider deliberately
A data residency requirement can rule out a provider with no region, or no mature-enough compliance certification, in the required location
questions.explain: Lesson 2's five real factors treat team expertise as a genuine cost, not an excuse, and the lesson is explicit that cost comparisons have to be workload-specific, not a general 'which cloud is cheaper' claim. Inherited multi-cloud from a merger is named as one of the honest reasons multi-cloud happens in practice, and data residency can genuinely rule a provider out. Accepting lock-in deliberately, in exchange for deeper integration, is explicitly called a legitimate choice, not a mistake to avoid at all costs.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 4, ________ is the path a request actually takes through a system, from the user through each tier to storage and back — the piece of an architecture diagram most often skipped, and the piece most likely to reveal a real design problem.
questions.explain: A real architecture diagram needs all three of network layout, compute tiers, and data flow to count as finished. Data flow is singled out as the one most often left out, because tracing how a request actually moves is what surfaces a tier reaching something it shouldn't, or a dependency creating a bottleneck, before any of it gets built.

questions.prompt: Put these deployment steps, from Lesson 5's real deployment order, in the correct sequence.
items: Create the resource group (or the account itself, for AWS)
Deploy compute and storage into the network
questions.explain: Each step is a hard dependency on the one before it, not a style preference: a subnet can't exist without a VNet to carve it from, an NSG attaches to a subnet or NIC that already has to exist, and a VM's network interface needs a subnet to request an address from. Skipping ahead to compute first just means tearing it down and rebuilding once the real network exists.

questions.code:
Under-planned: VPC sized at 10.0.0.0/24 (256 addresses total)
  -> One subnet barely fits. No room for a second tier, let alone five.

Planned with room to grow: VPC sized at 10.0.0.0/16 (65,536 addresses)
  -> snet-web   10.0.1.0/24
  -> snet-app   10.0.2.0/24
  -> snet-data  10.0.3.0/24
  -> (reserved) 10.0.4.0/24 through 10.0.255.0/24 for everything added later
questions.prompt: A VNet is sized at 10.0.0.0/16 and split into three /24 subnets, using only 10.0.1.0/24 through 10.0.3.0/24. Per Lesson 6, what's the real planning reason for leaving 10.0.4.0/24 through 10.0.255.0/24 unused?
options: To leave room for subnets that will be needed later — a monitoring tier, a backup/DR subnet, a second availability zone — without expanding the address space or redesigning the layout
Azure and AWS both require at least 250 unused /24 blocks to exist in every VNet or VPC by default
Unused address space directly reduces the monthly bill for the VNet or VPC
A /16 is the smallest CIDR block either cloud will accept for a VNet or VPC
questions.explain: Lesson 6's real planning question isn't how many addresses are needed today, it's how many subnets the environment will have in a year. Sizing the VNet at /16 instead of /24 leaves the later chapters — monitoring, backup/DR, a second AZ for high availability — their own ranges to use, instead of forcing a disruptive expansion or a full redesign once those needs show up.

questions.code:
# The common mistake — written "temporarily" during setup
az network nsg rule create \
  --resource-group rg-prod --nsg-name nsg-web \
  --name allow-everything --priority 100 \
  --source-address-prefixes '*' --destination-port-ranges '*' \
  --access Allow --protocol '*'
questions.prompt: Select every true statement about least-privilege NSG/security group rules, per Lesson 7.
options: Both Azure NSGs and AWS security groups deny all inbound traffic by default unless a rule explicitly allows it
A rule scoped to a specific CIDR range like 203.0.113.0/24 on one port takes the same number of commands to write as the wide-open rule shown above
Writing a wide-open rule "temporarily" during setup is a reliable way to get it tightened later once things are confirmed working
Each subnet or tier should get its own NSG or security group scoped to only the access that specific tier needs
A database tier's NSG allowing traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 is harmless as long as the application tier's own NSG is configured correctly
questions.explain: Both platforms deny all inbound traffic by default, and writing the narrow rule in the first place costs exactly the same number of commands as the wide-open one — the only difference is filling in the real source and port instead of a wildcard. A rule-per-tier is the whole design Lesson 7 builds toward. The "temporarily" open rule almost never actually gets tightened later under real deadline pressure, and a wide-open data-tier rule collapses the entire tiered design regardless of how correct the app tier's NSG is, since the database becomes reachable from anywhere.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 8, ________ is Azure's tool for tracing a specific path through NSGs and route tables and reporting exactly which rule allowed or blocked it, with AWS Reachability Analyzer as its equivalent.
questions.explain: Simple reachability checks (ping, Test-NetConnection, nc, curl) confirm whether a connection works, but Network Watcher's IP flow verify and connection troubleshoot features go further — they trace the actual path and name the specific rule responsible, which matters most once something fails and you need to know why, not just that it failed.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 9, what actually happens if you launch a VM or EC2 instance without specifying a subnet?
options: The platform silently substitutes a default — a brand-new VNet in Azure, or the account's default VPC and subnet in AWS — and the instance boots successfully on a network nobody designed
The launch command fails immediately with an error, and no instance is created
Azure and AWS both refuse to boot the instance until a VNet or VPC is manually attached after creation
The instance boots with no network interface at all, and can never be reached by anything
questions.explain: Omitting --vnet-name/--subnet or --subnet-id doesn't fail the launch — it quietly substitutes a default network. The instance boots fine, which is exactly the problem: it's running, looks correct, and is sitting on a network with none of the real NSG or security group rules from Chapter 2 applied to it, a gap that usually surfaces later as an unreachable or unexpectedly open instance.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B is the mix-up Lesson 9 specifically warns against — the launch doesn't fail at all, which is exactly what makes skipping the subnet flags dangerous. The platform quietly substitutes a default network instead of erroring out, so the mistake looks like a success rather than announcing itself.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about locking down a storage account or S3 bucket, per Lesson 10.
options: Setting --default-action Deny on an Azure storage account blocks every request by default, including from inside Azure, until a rule explicitly allows it
A brand-new S3 bucket is public by default until Block Public Access is explicitly turned on
S3's put-public-access-block with all four settings set to true guarantees no ACL, bucket policy, or cross-account grant can make the bucket public later
Creating a storage account or bucket successfully means its access configuration is also already correct
An Azure storage account network rule can scope access to one specific VNet/subnet instead of allowing requests from anywhere
questions.explain: A storage account's --default-action Deny blocks everything until a rule opens a specific path, and put-public-access-block is the explicit, account-level guarantee that nothing configured later can make the bucket public. A network rule scopes that one opening to a specific VNet/subnet, like the app tier's. New S3 buckets already default to private, not public, and creating the resource successfully says nothing about whether its access configuration is actually correct — that's the whole point of Lesson 10's warning.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 11, an EC2 ________ is the AWS mechanism that attaches an IAM role, and its temporary STS credentials, to a running instance — with no access key ever sitting in a config file.
questions.explain: An instance profile wraps the IAM role and attaches it to the running instance, the same job a system-assigned managed identity does on Azure. Either way, the application authenticates through the compute resource's own identity, so there's no embedded credential anywhere in the chain for anyone to leak, commit, or forget to rotate.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of Lesson 12's smoke test in the order they're actually run.
items: Write a test file and upload it to storage using the VM's identity
Download the uploaded file back and confirm it matches
Check the application's own health endpoint with curl
Conclude the environment is genuinely working, not just running
questions.explain: The storage round trip confirms Lesson 9's network path and Lesson 11's identity grant both work; the service health check then confirms the application itself is actually running, not just that the VM is reachable. Only after both checks pass does the environment count as deployed and working, rather than merely running.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly explains why a newly deployed environment counts as 'flying blind,' per Lesson 13, even though Azure Monitor or CloudWatch is already collecting platform metrics?
options: Nothing is watching those metrics, nothing notifies anyone when a threshold is crossed, and application/OS logs aren't flowing anywhere centralized yet — the metrics existing isn't the same as monitoring being stood up
Azure Monitor and CloudWatch don't actually start collecting any data until an alert rule is manually created first
Platform metrics only become visible once a support ticket is opened with the cloud provider
"Flying blind" only applies to environments that have no compute resources deployed yet
questions.explain: The moment Chapters 1-3's resources existed, the platform started collecting their metrics automatically — that part needs no setup. What's still missing is visibility, notification, and a centralized log destination, which is exactly what standing up monitoring closes. The gap 'flying blind' describes is in watching and acting on the data, not in whether the data exists.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B reverses cause and effect — Lesson 13 is explicit that Azure Monitor/CloudWatch starts collecting platform metrics automatically the moment a resource exists, with no alert rule required first. The real gap is visibility and notification, not data collection itself.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the alerts that actually matter for a new deployment, per Lesson 14.
options: Resource thresholds, failed health checks, and security-relevant events are the three categories that cover almost everything worth alerting on for a new deployment
A basic deployment genuinely needs an alert configured for every metric the platform makes visible
An alert rule with no Action Group or SNS topic attached is functionally as useless as having no alert at all
Repeated failed authentication attempts belong in the security-relevant events category, separate from resource load
A sustained-high-CPU alert should fire on any brief spike above the threshold, even one lasting only a few seconds
questions.explain: Lesson 14's whole argument is that alerting on every available metric creates noise, not safety — the four-alert worked example deliberately covers only resource thresholds, failed health checks, and security-relevant events. An alert with no notification wired to it never reaches anyone, which makes it as useless as no alert. The CPU alert is specifically defined as sustained (e.g. 15 minutes), not a brief normal spike, precisely to avoid firing on unremarkable load.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: ________ is the point where alerts fire so often for non-problems that people start ignoring alerts in general, including the ones that actually matter.
questions.explain: Alert fatigue isn't something that happens only to an analyst reading a flood of alerts — Lesson 15 traces it back to the configuration side, where setting a threshold too sensitively on day one guarantees the exact flood that trains people to dismiss notifications without reading them.

questions.prompt: Match each item on Lesson 16's five-point monitoring checklist to what it actually verifies.
right: Resources are confirmed visible in the portal or CLI reporting into the log destination, not just technically eligible to
The small, high-confidence alert set exists as real alert rules against real resources, not just planned on paper
A test condition was deliberately triggered to confirm the notification actually arrives end to end, not just that the rule is syntactically valid
A single view shows the handful of metrics that matter in one place, so a quick glance answers whether everything is normal
questions.explain: The checklist exists because it's easy to think monitoring is 'done' once a few things are set up, when some of those pieces were only ever configured, never actually verified. Each point checks a different gap: data really flowing, rules really existing, notifications really arriving, and a single place to glance at all of it.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes RTO from RPO, per Lesson 17?
options: RTO measures how long a system can be down before that's unacceptable; RPO measures how much data loss, in time, is acceptable if you have to restore from a backup
RTO measures acceptable data loss in time, while RPO measures acceptable downtime
RTO and RPO both measure the exact same thing, just using different units
RTO is set by the backup schedule a team already has, and RPO is set by the business afterward to match it
A workload can only ever have a tight RTO and a tight RPO together, never one tight and the other loose
questions.explain: RTO is about tolerable downtime; RPO is about tolerable data loss, measured as how old the last good backup is allowed to be. A static marketing site can have a tight RTO (down looks bad) but a loose RPO (losing a day of edits doesn't hurt much), which is exactly why the two numbers have to be set independently and honestly for the specific workload in front of you.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B swaps the two definitions entirely — it's RTO that measures acceptable downtime and RPO that measures acceptable data loss, not the reverse. Confusing which number measures which kind of failure leads to configuring the wrong thing: backup frequency answers RPO, restore speed answers RTO.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about backup policy and retention, per Lesson 18.
options: Tiered retention — dense recently, sparser further back — covers the same total time span as keeping every daily backup forever, at a fraction of the storage cost
Keeping every backup forever is the safest retention policy, because storage cost doesn't actually matter
A production database with a 1-hour RPO and a dev/test VM that gets rebuilt from a template every sprint should generally use the same backup policy
AWS Backup can manage backup rules and lifecycle across EBS volumes, RDS databases, and other supported resources from one place
An Azure Backup policy defines both how often backups run and how long each one is retained
questions.explain: Tiered retention (daily for a week, weekly for a month, monthly for a year) is the real-world pattern precisely because it covers the same span as keeping everything daily, at a fraction of the storage. AWS Backup's whole value is centralizing rules and lifecycle across resource types, and an Azure Backup policy bundles frequency and retention together. Keeping everything forever is explicitly called neither free nor sensible, and a policy isn't 'set once, apply everywhere' — a production database's 1-hour RPO and a disposable dev/test VM need fundamentally different policies.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a ________ means actually restoring a backup into a real environment and verifying the result — the only way to know a backup is genuinely good, since a job reporting 'completed successfully' doesn't confirm the data can be restored.
questions.explain: A backup job's success status only confirms the backup process ran without error. It says nothing about whether the result is complete, uncorrupted, or missing a dependency it needs to restore cleanly — which is exactly why a restore test, run on a real cadence, is the only thing that turns 'we have backups' into 'we have backups we know work.'

questions.prompt: Match each piece of a small-environment disaster recovery plan to what it actually covers, per Lesson 20.
right: Agreed on ahead of time for each system, not guessed at during the incident
Backups frequent enough and retained long enough to actually satisfy the agreed RPO
Proof, on a real cadence, that a restore actually works rather than an assumption based on a green checkmark
Written steps naming who restores what, in what order, and who they notify during a real outage
questions.explain: Lesson 20's honest scope for a job-ready cloud engineer is these four pieces, not an enterprise architect's multi-region failover design. Each piece closes a different gap: knowing the numbers, having a policy that meets them, proving the backups actually work, and writing down who does what so a 2 AM outage isn't improvised for the first time under pressure.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes what a 'bus factor of 1' means for a deployed environment, per Lesson 21?
options: Only one person understands how the environment is wired together, so the team loses the ability to safely operate or change it the moment that person is unavailable
The environment can tolerate exactly one server failure before an outage occurs
Exactly one documented runbook exists for the environment, which is considered sufficient
The environment has exactly one subnet, which is a networking anti-pattern
Bus factor measures how many simultaneous users the environment can support
questions.explain: Bus factor is about knowledge, not infrastructure — a deployment can have perfectly redundant servers and still have a bus factor of 1 if the NSG rules, subnet layout, and alert thresholds all live only in one engineer's head. Lesson 21's vacation scenario shows exactly what that costs: a twenty-minute fix turning into two days once the one person who understood the environment is unreachable.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B confuses bus factor with infrastructure redundancy — bus factor describes people and knowledge, not servers or networking. An environment with fully redundant compute can still have a bus factor of 1 if only one person actually understands how it's configured and why.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the relationship between an architecture diagram and a runbook, per Lesson 22.
options: A diagram shows what exists and how it's laid out; a runbook covers how to operate and troubleshoot it day to day
A runbook step like "check web-vm-01 through web-vm-03" is immediately useful even to someone who has never seen the architecture diagram
The diagram gives the runbook its context, which is why the two are written together rather than as separate projects weeks apart
A runbook replaces the need for an architecture diagram once it's written
A useful runbook names the specific common tasks, who to contact, and exactly where logs live for each major component
questions.explain: The diagram answers 'what is this and how is it laid out,' the runbook answers 'how do I operate and fix it' — neither replaces the other. A runbook step naming three VMs only makes immediate sense to someone who can glance at the diagram and see those VMs sitting behind a load balancer in a specific subnet; without that picture it's just names and commands with no mental map, which is exactly why the two get written together.

questions.prompt: Match each item on Lesson 24's handoff checklist to the real problem it exists to prevent.
right: An out-of-date diagram being trusted by default even though subnets have been added or a VM has been resized since it was drawn
The new owner having no specific reference for common tasks, contacts, or log locations, and having to hunt for answers during an outage
The new owner being able to read the diagram but not actually log in to the portal to act on anything
An alert still paging the person who's leaving, so it goes nowhere, or goes to someone who can no longer act on it
questions.explain: Lesson 24 ties each checklist item to a specific, real failure it prevents — an out-of-date diagram being trusted anyway, a missing runbook forcing a hunt mid-incident, access described but never actually granted, and alerts routing to someone who's already gone. Treating the list as a gate, not a formality, means none of those gaps survives the handoff.

questions.prompt: Match each of Lesson 25's five places a new deployment usually breaks to its real example.
right: A resource sitting in the wrong subnet, with no route to the internet gateway
A rule that's gone stale, like an office IP range that moved since the rule was originally written
A private DNS zone that isn't linked to the VNet that needs it
A managed identity or user role missing the one permission a new feature now depends on
A subscription or account that's quietly hit a vCPU or IP address ceiling, failing with no obvious configuration error
questions.explain: These five aren't five unrelated failure modes — they're the layers a request actually passes through, roughly in order: network, firewall rule, name resolution, identity, and capacity. Almost every vague 'it's broken' ticket turns out to be one of these five wearing a different costume, which is exactly why knowing the list in advance turns a long guessing session into a short checklist.

questions.prompt: Put Lesson 26's five-question connectivity diagnostic sequence in the order it's actually run.
items: Is there a route to it?
Is the firewall/NSG/security group actually allowing this traffic?
Is the service actually listening on the expected port?
questions.explain: The order runs from the broadest, cheapest thing to check toward the narrowest, most expensive one, mirroring the same layered logic the networking fundamentals course built with the OSI model. The sequence also tells you when to stop: the moment one question fails, that's the root cause, and there's no need to keep checking the layers after it.

questions.prompt: A request comes back with "Forbidden" / 403. Which statement correctly explains what that error text tells you, per Lesson 27?
options: The request reached the resource and was deliberately refused — this is a permission problem, not a network, firewall, or DNS problem
The request never got a response from anything, which means it's almost always a network or firewall problem
"Forbidden" and "Connection timed out" indicate the identical root cause, just logged with different wording
A 403 always means the resource itself has crashed or stopped responding
questions.explain: Getting an actual "Forbidden" answer back means the network worked fine and the request reached its target — it was refused on purpose, by an identity lacking the right permission. That single distinction (an answer that says no, versus no answer at all) is the fastest triage step available, and it points straight at a role or policy gap, not at Lesson 26's connectivity sequence.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes what a timeout or 'no route to host' error means, not a 403 — Lesson 27 is explicit that a genuine 'Forbidden' response means the network and firewall layers already worked, and it was the identity's lack of permission that caused the refusal, the opposite of a connectivity failure.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 28, ________ means reverting to the last known-good state — fast and usually a single command, but it doesn't actually fix the underlying root cause, which stays there waiting to resurface.
questions.explain: Rolling back trades a fix for speed: it returns the system to a state you've already verified works, but the stale rule, missing permission, or quota issue that actually caused the incident is still sitting there, unresolved, until someone fixes forward later.

questions.prompt: For Harrow Peak Outfitters' app VM, you pull a month of CPU and memory utilization off the old physical server before choosing Standard_D2s_v5 for its replacement. Per Lesson 29, what does this actually demonstrate?
options: Right-sizing from real observed usage instead of guessing or padding the size "to be safe," the same discipline Chapter 1 teaches
That Azure requires a month of historical usage data before any VM can be created
That Standard_D2s_v5 is the only VM size Azure offers for a company of this size
That the old physical server's specs become irrelevant once the workload moves to the cloud
questions.explain: Pulling real utilization numbers off the server that's actually been running the workload, instead of guessing or defaulting to something large 'to be safe,' is exactly Chapter 1's sizing discipline applied for real — landing on a size with enough headroom for the real peak, not padded for an imaginary one.

questions.prompt: During final testing, a blob upload for Harrow Peak returns a 403. A connection test to the storage endpoint succeeds, and the managed identity's Storage Blob Data Contributor role assignment is confirmed correct. Per Lesson 31, what should you check next, and why?
options: The storage account's own network rules — its firewall was set to allow only selected virtual networks, and mgmt-subnet had been added to that list by mistake instead of app-subnet
Nothing further — a confirmed role assignment means the 403 must be a transient error that will resolve on its own
The VM's operating system firewall, since Azure RBAC and storage network rules can never cause a 403 once a role is assigned
The database's connection string, since a 403 on a blob upload always indicates a SQL authentication failure
questions.explain: Confirming the connection succeeds rules out network-down, and confirming the role assignment rules out a missing RBAC grant — which means the cause has to be a third layer, not either of those two. The storage account's own network rules, restricted to selected virtual networks, turned out to have the wrong subnet on the allow list, a mistake made during buildout that only a systematic, layer-by-layer check like Chapter 7's would catch.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 30, why does granting harrowpeak-app-vm's managed identity the Storage Blob Data Contributor role eliminate an entire category of risk that a stored access key never fully removes, even if that key is rotated regularly?
options: There is no credential at all to leak, expire, or get copied into a repo by accident — the VM authenticates as itself, so rotation discipline becomes irrelevant rather than just well-managed
Storage Blob Data Contributor is a stronger role than any role a stored access key could ever be granted
Managed identities make the storage account's network firewall rules unnecessary
A regularly rotated access key is already just as secure as a managed identity, so the real benefit is purely organizational
questions.explain: A stored key, however diligently rotated, is still a secret that exists somewhere and can be leaked, committed, or copied by mistake in the window before the next rotation. A managed identity removes that category of risk entirely rather than managing it well, because there's no credential sitting in a config file for anyone to mishandle in the first place — which is exactly why Lesson 31's 403 incident traced back to a network rule, not a leaked or stale credential.
